title: LINUX DEEP DIVE
description: Go beyond the command line: /proc internals, file permissions, SUID/SGID bits, seccomp, systemd unit types, process signalling, and shell redirection. Built for operators who need to own a system, not just use one.

links.text: explainshell — Break down any shell command

questions.question: Which /proc file contains the command line of process with PID 1337?
questions.explanation: /proc/<PID>/cmdline holds the null-separated command-line arguments of the process. /proc/<PID>/maps shows memory mappings.

questions.question: What octal permission value gives the owner read/write/execute and the group and others read/execute only?
Which systemd unit type runs a command once on boot and does not restart?
questions.explanation: Type=oneshot executes the ExecStart command synchronously and is considered active only while the process runs, then exits.

questions.question: In Linux, what does the sticky bit on a directory do?

options.B: Prevents users from deleting files owned by others in that directory
options.C: Causes the directory to be loaded into RAM on mount
options.D: Inherits the owner's UID for all new files

questions.explanation: The sticky bit (chmod +t) on a directory (like /tmp) lets users delete only their own files, even if they have write permission to the directory.

questions.question: Which command shows all open file descriptors for a specific process?
questions.explanation: `lsof -p <pid>` lists all open files (including sockets and pipes) for the given process ID.

questions.question: What does `chmod u+s /usr/bin/myprog` accomplish?

options.A: Makes the file executable only by root
options.B: Sets the SUID bit so the program runs with the file owner's privileges
options.C: Adds the sticky bit to restrict deletion
options.D: Grants setgid so the program runs with the group's privileges

questions.explanation: SUID (Set User ID) on an executable causes it to run with the file owner's UID instead of the invoking user's UID.

questions.question: Which kernel facility allows filtering and restriction of system calls a process can make?
questions.explanation: seccomp (Secure Computing Mode) restricts the set of system calls a process may make, used heavily in container runtimes.

questions.question: How do you send a signal to all processes in a process group with PGID 4242?
questions.explanation: Prefixing the PID with a minus sign (`-4242`) tells kill to target the entire process group. `-TERM` can be omitted as it's the default.

questions.question: In bash, what is the difference between `2>&1` and `&>`?

options.A: They are identical in all shells
options.B: `2>&1` redirects stderr to stdout; `&>` redirects both to a file (bash-specific)
options.D: `2>&1` suppresses all output; `&>` appends to a file

questions.explanation: `2>&1` redirects file descriptor 2 (stderr) to wherever fd 1 (stdout) currently points. `&> file` is bash shorthand to redirect both stdout and stderr to a file.

questions.question: Which /etc file maps usernames to UID, GID, home directory, and login shell?
questions.explanation: /etc/passwd holds one record per user: username:password-placeholder:UID:GID:GECOS:home:shell. Passwords are in /etc/shadow.
